name: PE / Windows executable
explanation: Every Windows Portable Executable (PE) binary begins with the two-byte 'MZ' signature (0x4D 0x5A) which is the IMAGE_DOS_HEADER.e_magic field, named after Mark Zbikowski. The bytes that follow form the rest of the DOS stub plus a 4-byte offset at file offset 0x3C (e_lfanew) that points to the IMAGE_NT_HEADERS where the actual PE header lives. So when you see 'MZ' at offset 0 you are looking at .exe, .dll, .sys, .efi, .scr, or any other Windows-loadable image; the variant comes from the PE header that the e_lfanew offset reveals.

name: ELF / Unix-like executable
explanation: Linux, BSD, and Solaris executables begin with the four-byte ELF magic (0x7F followed by 'ELF'). Byte 4 says 32-bit (0x01) or 64-bit (0x02); byte 5 is endianness (0x01 little, 0x02 big); byte 6 is ELF version (always 0x01 today); byte 7 is OS ABI. After a 16-byte e_ident block, e_type at offset 16 says executable (ET_EXEC = 0x02), shared object (ET_DYN = 0x03), relocatable (ET_REL = 0x01), or core (ET_CORE = 0x04). Modern PIE binaries are ET_DYN even though they are 'executables' from the user perspective; check the INTERP segment to disambiguate.

name: Mach-O 64-bit (macOS executable)
explanation: macOS 64-bit Mach-O binaries begin with the magic 0xFEEDFACF in big-endian order, which on disk is 'CF FA ED FE' little-endian. The 32-bit variant uses 0xFEEDFACE / 'CE FA ED FE'. The bytes that follow encode CPU type (e.g. 0x01000007 = x86_64, 0x0100000C = ARM64), CPU subtype, file type (MH_EXECUTE = 0x02, MH_DYLIB = 0x06, MH_BUNDLE = 0x08), number of load commands, and load command size. Universal / fat binaries that bundle multiple architectures begin with 0xCAFEBABE ('CA FE BA BE') which is also Java class-file magic, so context matters.

name: ZIP / Office Open XML / JAR / APK
explanation: The ZIP format starts with 'PK' followed by a 2-byte record type (0x0304 = local file header, 0x0102 = central directory, 0x0506 = end-of-central-directory). Modern Microsoft Office files (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) are ZIP containers whose first entry is the [Content_Types].xml part; Java JARs and Android APKs are also ZIPs. So 'PK 03 04' alone says 'this is a ZIP container' but does not say which kind. Look at the path of the first inner entry, or look for 'word/' (DOCX), 'xl/' (XLSX), 'META-INF/MANIFEST.MF' (JAR), 'AndroidManifest.xml' (APK).

name: PDF document
explanation: PDFs begin with '%PDF-' followed by a version string ('1.4', '1.7', '2.0'). The %PDF- header may not literally be at offset 0 if the file has a UTF-8 BOM or other prefix bytes, but most parsers tolerate up to 1024 bytes of leading garbage by spec. PDFs of interest in cybersec usually carry malicious JavaScript via the /JavaScript or /JS keys in the object dictionary, embedded files via /EmbeddedFile, or launch actions via /Launch. The file ends with '%%EOF' and may have multiple trailers due to incremental updates; look for '%PDF-' near the start AND '%%EOF' near the end to confirm structure.

name: OLE2 compound document (legacy Office, MSI)
hex_at_offset_0: D0 CF 11 E0 A1 B1 1A E1
explanation: The OLE2 / Compound File Binary format magic is 0xD0CF11E0A1B11AE1 (a binary palindrome around 0xE0). It is the container format for legacy Office (.doc, .xls, .ppt before 2007), Microsoft Installer packages (.msi), Windows shortcut files (.lnk, sometimes), and several other Microsoft formats. From an attacker's perspective the OLE2 container is interesting because it can carry VBA macros, OLE-embedded payloads, and exploit shellcode in malformed streams. Distinguishing the inner format requires reading the root entry's CLSID and the named streams.

name: PNG image
explanation: PNG starts with an 8-byte signature: 0x89 (high-bit set, breaks 7-bit text systems), 'PNG' (the format), CRLF (line-ending sanity check), 0x1A (DOS EOF), LF. After the signature the file is a chain of length-tag-data-CRC chunks; the first chunk is always IHDR (header). PNGs are interesting in cybersec because of steganography (LSB-encoded data in pixel bytes), 'polyglot' files that are both a PNG and a ZIP, and historical bugs in libpng allowing memory disclosure. Look for unusually large IDAT chunks or text chunks (tEXt, iTXt) with binary-looking content for steganography.

name: UPX-packed binary signature
explanation: UPX is the most common open-source PE / ELF / Mach-O packer. A UPX-packed binary keeps its original PE / ELF header but the section table contains sections named 'UPX0' (0x55 0x50 0x58 0x30, an empty section that will hold the unpacked code), 'UPX1' (the packed body), and 'UPX2' / '.rsrc' for resources. The 'UPX!' marker (0x55 0x50 0x58 0x21) appears later in the file as part of the UPX header structure that the unpacking stub reads at runtime. Detection: look at section names. False positive rate is near-zero because legitimate compilers do not emit sections named 'UPX0' / 'UPX1'.

name: Themida / VMProtect signs of obfuscation
longer_pattern: (typical Themida section: '.themida' or '.taggant'; VMProtect uses '.vmp0' / '.vmp1' / '.vmp2' section names)
explanation: Commercial protectors Themida (Oreans) and VMProtect leave specific named sections in the PE that survive unless the operator strips them. Themida-packed binaries typically contain '.themida' or '.taggant' sections; VMProtect uses '.vmp0', '.vmp1', '.vmp2'. They also produce extremely large entry-point dispatcher routines (10K+ instructions of branching and constant-folding obfuscation), high entropy in the code section (>7.0 bits per byte versus ~5.5 for normal compiled C++), and frequent CPUID / RDTSC / IsDebuggerPresent calls in the unpacker stub. Detection at offset 0 is fragile; reach for entropy + section name + import table patterns.

name: NOP sled (x86)
explanation: A sequence of 0x90 bytes is the x86 single-byte NOP instruction. Attackers prepend a NOP sled to shellcode to widen the landing zone for an imprecise return-address overwrite: as long as control flow lands anywhere in the sled, execution slides forward instruction-by-instruction until it hits the actual payload. Modern variants use 'pseudo-NOPs' that are non-90 instructions which still preserve the architectural state (e.g. 0x40 = inc eax, 0x48 = dec eax in 32-bit mode) to evade signature-based detection. Long runs of 0x90 in a buffer that is not normally code (a network packet payload, a file upload buffer) are a strong signal.

name: x64 function prologue
explanation: A canonical x86_64 function prologue: 0x55 (push rbp), 0x48 0x89 0xE5 (mov rbp, rsp), 0x48 0x83 0xEC 0x?? (sub rsp, N) where N is the local-variable stack size, then 0x48 0x89 0x7D 0xF8 (mov [rbp-8], rdi) which saves the first integer argument. Recognising this pattern by eye is fundamental to manual reversing: it tells you you are at a function entry, the local frame size is the byte that follows 'sub rsp', and the calling convention is System V AMD64 (rdi = arg1, rsi = arg2, rdx = arg3, rcx = arg4, r8 = arg5, r9 = arg6). Microsoft x64 passes args in rcx/rdx/r8/r9 instead.
examples: objdump -d output of a compiled C function

name: Linux x64 syscall pattern
explanation: On Linux x86_64, system calls are issued via the SYSCALL instruction (0x0F 0x05) after loading the syscall number into rax. Common patterns in shellcode: '48 31 C0 B0 3B' (xor rax,rax; mov al, 0x3B = execve), '48 31 FF' (xor rdi, rdi to zero out arg1), 'B8 01 00 00 00 0F 05' (mov eax, 1 = write, then syscall). Recognising 0x0F 0x05 in an unexpected location (a network buffer, a heap allocation that should hold data) is a strong signal that shellcode is present. Static analysis tools key on this; sandboxes hook the SYSCALL instruction in user-mode for instrumentation.

name: PE Optional Header Magic (PE32 vs PE32+)
explanation: Inside the IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER (which despite its name is mandatory for executable PEs), the first WORD is the Magic field: 0x010B for 32-bit images (PE32) and 0x020B for 64-bit images (PE32+). Note the byte order on disk is little-endian, so 0x010B appears as '0B 01' and 0x020B as '0B 02'. This field is the disambiguator between IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER32 and IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 layouts; the 64-bit variant is 16 bytes longer because BaseOfData is removed and ImageBase / SizeOfStackReserve / SizeOfStackCommit / SizeOfHeapReserve / SizeOfHeapCommit grow to 8 bytes each. A PE viewer that misreads this field corrupts every subsequent offset.
examples: the Magic field readable via Hex Workshop or HxD

name: PE Machine field (architecture)
explanation: The IMAGE_FILE_HEADER.Machine field at the start of the PE header (right after the 'PE\0\0' signature) declares the target architecture. Common values: 0x014C (IMAGE_FILE_MACHINE_I386 = 32-bit x86), 0x8664 (AMD64 = 64-bit x86), 0xAA64 (ARM64), 0x01C4 (ARMNT = 32-bit ARM Thumb-2), 0x0200 (Itanium IA64, deprecated). Reading this field tells you which disassembler / debugger to attach. Attackers occasionally manipulate this field (or the corresponding ELF e_machine) to confuse static analysis tools that key on it for unpacker-arch selection.
examples: a 32-bit malware sample on a 64-bit host (run via WoW64)
ARM64 mobile malware compiled for newer Macs

name: Linux x64 execve('/bin/sh') shellcode
explanation: A compact 28-byte Linux x86_64 execve('/bin/sh', NULL, NULL) shellcode. Decoded: 'xor rax, rax' (zero rax), 'push rax' (push the null terminator that '/bin/sh\0' will reference), 'mov rbx, 0x0068732F6E69622F' (the string '/bin/sh' little-endian-encoded), 'push rbx', 'mov rdi, rsp' (rdi points at '/bin/sh'), 'xor rdx, rdx' (envp = NULL), 'xor rsi, rsi' (argv = NULL), 'mov al, 0x3B' (sys_execve number), 'syscall'. Recognising this exact byte string is one of the canonical IDS signatures for stage-2 shellcode landing in memory. Variants permute the register-zeroing instructions or use alphanumeric encoders to evade naive pattern matchers.
examples: a stage-1 dropper that executes after a stack overflow

name: JPEG image
explanation: Every JPEG begins with the SOI marker 0xFFD8 followed by another 0xFF byte. Common variants: FF D8 FF E0 = JFIF (most common), FF D8 FF E1 = EXIF (most camera photos), FF D8 FF E8 = SPIFF, FF D8 FF DB = raw JPEG with quantization tables. JPEG files always END with the EOI marker FF D9. Useful to know: malware polyglots sometimes hide payload between FF D9 and EOF since most viewers stop reading at EOI.
examples: any photo from a phone or camera

name: GIF image
explanation: GIF files start with 'GIF87a' (47 49 46 38 37 61) or 'GIF89a' (47 49 46 38 39 61). 89a added animation, interlacing, transparency. The next 4 bytes are the logical screen width and height as little-endian uint16. Used historically for animated images; mostly replaced by APNG / WebP / video formats but still ubiquitous on the web.

name: MP4 / QuickTime container
explanation: MP4 / MOV / 3GP containers are organized as 'atoms' or 'boxes'. The first atom is always 'ftyp' (file-type) starting at offset 4, with a length header in the first 4 bytes. The brand at offset 8 (BB BB BB BB) tells you the variant: 'isom' = generic ISO base, 'mp42' = MPEG-4 v2, 'qt  ' (with two spaces) = QuickTime, 'M4A ' = audio-only AAC, '3gp4' = 3GPP.

name: Java class file
explanation: Java compiled .class files begin with the magic 0xCAFEBABE. Bytes 4-5 are minor version, 6-7 are major version: 0x34 = Java 8, 0x37 = Java 11, 0x3D = Java 17, 0x41 = Java 21. After that comes the constant pool. Mach-O FAT (universal) binaries also use CAFEBABE at offset 0, distinguished by checking the next 4 bytes: a Mach-O FAT has the count of architectures, a Java class has the version.

name: WebAssembly module
explanation: WASM binary modules begin with 0x00 followed by 'asm' (0x61 0x73 0x6D), then a 4-byte little-endian version (currently 0x01000000 for v1). After the magic + version come typed sections (type, import, function, table, memory, global, export, start, element, code, data) each with a 1-byte ID. Used in browsers, Cloudflare Workers, smart contracts (NEAR, Polkadot).

name: GZIP compressed
longer_pattern: 1F 8B 08 NN MM MM MM MM ZZ FF
explanation: GZIP starts with 1F 8B (signature) then 0x08 (DEFLATE compression method, the only one defined). Byte 3 is flags (FTEXT, FHCRC, FEXTRA, FNAME, FCOMMENT). Bytes 4-7 are the modification time as Unix epoch LE. Byte 9 is the OS the archive was created on (0x03 = Unix, 0x0A = TOPS/20, 0xFF = unknown). After the header comes a DEFLATE stream; .tar.gz is GZIP wrapping a TAR archive.
examples: firmware blob in a router image

name: SQLite database
explanation: SQLite databases begin with the literal 16-byte string 'SQLite format 3' followed by a null byte. Used by iOS + Android system databases (SMS, contacts, browser history), Firefox / Chrome bookmarks + cookies, app caches everywhere. Forensically valuable: a recovered .db file is queryable with the sqlite3 CLI even if the original app is gone. Use `strings` and `sqlite3 file '.dump'` to extract content.

name: Android DEX bytecode
explanation: Android Dalvik / ART executables (.dex inside an APK) begin with 'dex\n' (64 65 78 0A) followed by a 3-byte version + null. '035' is the historical default; '038' is Android 8+; '039' adds new opcodes. APK files are ZIP archives so they start with PK\x03\x04 (BIN-004); the DEX inside is at /classes.dex. Extract via `apktool` or `unzip`, then `dex2jar` + JADX for source.

name: x86 execve('/bin/sh') shellcode (Linux 32-bit)
explanation:
Classic Linux x86 execve('/bin/sh') stub. Decoded:
  xor eax, eax           ; eax = 0
  push eax               ; null terminator
  push 0x68732f2f        ; '//sh'
  push 0x6e69622f        ; '/bin'
  mov ebx, esp           ; ebx = pointer to '/bin//sh'
  push eax               ; null argv terminator
  push ebx               ; argv[0]
  mov ecx, esp           ; ecx = argv
  mov al, 11             ; sys_execve
  int 0x80               ; syscall
23 bytes, no nulls (so it survives strcpy). The double-slash in '//sh' is a no-op the kernel tolerates and gives the assembler a 4-byte aligned string to push.

name: ARM64 function prologue
explanation:
ARM64 function prologue, save frame pointer and link register, set new frame pointer:
  stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!  ; FD 7B BF A9
  mov x29, sp                ; FD 03 00 91
All ARM64 instructions are 4 bytes and little-endian encoded. The pattern A9 BF 7B FD = stp x29, x30 with pre-decrement of sp by 16 is essentially universal at the start of any ARM64 function. Apple Silicon, modern Android, AWS Graviton all decode this.

name: x64 function epilogue
longer_pattern: C9 C3 (or 5D C3 if no enter)
explanation:
Standard x86_64 function epilogue:
  pop rbp        ; 5D — restore caller's frame ptr
  ret            ; C3 — return to caller
Or with the legacy `leave` instruction:
  leave          ; C9 — equivalent of mov rsp,rbp + pop rbp
  ret            ; C3
Together with the prologue (push rbp / mov rbp, rsp = 55 48 89 E5) these bracket every C function. Modern compilers omit the prologue/epilogue for leaf functions with no stack frame, so absence doesn't mean it's not a function.
examples: Last bytes of any x86_64 function

name: ROP gadget pop rdi; ret
explanation: x86_64 ROP gadget that pops a value from the stack into rdi (the System V AMD64 first-argument register), then returns. Combined with the address of system() and a string '/bin/sh', forms a minimal ret2libc chain that spawns a shell. Found via `ROPgadget --binary ...` or `ropper`. The two-byte sequence is so common in any compiled binary (every function ending pops rdi at some point) that gadget hunters always find it.

name: x64 reverse shell connect-stub start
explanation:
First lines of a Linux x64 reverse-shell shellcode, calling sys_socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0) (syscall number 41 = 0x29):
  push 0x29; pop rax       ; rax = 41 (socket)
  cdq                       ; rdx = 0
  push 2; pop rdi           ; rdi = AF_INET
  push 1; pop rsi           ; rsi = SOCK_STREAM
  syscall
After the socket comes connect() to a hardcoded addr+port, dup2() of the socket onto stdin/stdout/stderr, then execve('/bin/sh'). The push-pop constants pattern keeps the bytes printable and null-free for surviving string copies.

name: PE Import Address Table (IAT) signature
explanation: PE binaries resolve external functions through the Import Directory in the .idata section. Look for ASCII strings like 'kernel32.dll', 'ntdll.dll', 'CreateFileA', 'VirtualAlloc', 'GetProcAddress'. Suspicious imports for malware analysis: VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread (process injection); WinHttpOpen + WinHttpConnect (C2); CryptEncrypt + CryptGenKey (ransomware). PEview / CFF Explorer / `strings` shows them; pe-bear gives a parsed view.

name: ELF PT_LOAD segment marker
explanation: ELF program headers describe how the kernel loader maps the binary into memory. PT_LOAD (p_type = 1) marks a segment to load; p_flags tells you R, W, X permissions. Most binaries have one R-X PT_LOAD (code) and one R-W PT_LOAD (data + bss). Modern PIE binaries also have a PT_DYNAMIC segment (p_type = 2) for the dynamic linker. A PT_LOAD with WX flags together is suspicious — usually means JIT or unpacker.

name: ELF dynamic interpreter (PT_INTERP)
explanation: Dynamically-linked ELF binaries embed the path to their dynamic linker in the PT_INTERP segment. Standard paths: /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 (glibc x86_64), /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1 (musl x86_64), /system/bin/linker64 (Android). Statically-linked binaries have no PT_INTERP — `file` reports 'statically linked'. Custom interpreter strings are a known anti-forensics technique to break analysis tools.

name: PE Section .text characteristics
explanation: Every PE has a .text section (8-byte name field, null-padded). Its Characteristics field is at offset +36 in the section header. 0x60000020 = IMAGE_SCN_CNT_CODE | IMAGE_SCN_MEM_EXECUTE | IMAGE_SCN_MEM_READ. Other common section names: .rdata (read-only data), .data (writable data), .rsrc (resources, icons, version info), .reloc (relocations). Suspicious: .text section that is also writable (RWX); custom section names like '.evil' or high-entropy section names.

name: Base64 encoded data
explanation: Base64 encodes 3 bytes of binary as 4 ASCII chars from the set [A-Za-z0-9+/], padded with '=' to a multiple of 4 chars. Output length = ceil(input_bytes / 3) * 4. Recognise: long ASCII strings ending in 0, 1, or 2 '=' signs. Variants: URL-safe Base64 swaps + and / for - and _. Used for encoding binary in JSON, JWT payloads, embedded images in HTML (data URLs), and obfuscating shellcode. Decode with `base64 -d` (coreutils) or `python3 -c "import base64; print(base64.b64decode('...'))"`.

name: Hex string (textual representation)
longer_pattern: deadbeef or DE AD BE EF or \xde\xad\xbe\xef
explanation: Hex strings encode binary as 2 ASCII chars per byte from [0-9a-fA-F]. Length is always even. Recognise: long-ish strings that match the regex. Variants: space-separated 'DE AD BE EF', backslash-x prefix '\xde\xad\xbe\xef' (C / Python), 0x prefix per byte '0xde, 0xad'. Used for representing hashes, byte arrays in source code, network packet dumps. Decode with `xxd -r -p`, `python3 -c "print(bytes.fromhex('...'))"`, or just paste into CyberChef.

name: UTF-8 BOM (byte order mark)
explanation: Some Windows tools (Notepad, older Excel) prepend EF BB BF to UTF-8 files as a BOM. UTF-8 doesn't actually need a BOM (it's encoded the same regardless of byte order), but the bytes mean 'this is UTF-8' to anything that checks. Causes problems: shell scripts with a BOM fail because the BOM bytes are not whitespace; Python 3 handles them silently with `encoding='utf-8-sig'`. UTF-16 BOM is FF FE (LE) or FE FF (BE), which is more important because the byte order matters.

name: MD5 hex digest length recognition
explanation: MD5 produces a 128-bit (16-byte) hash. As a hex string it's exactly 32 lowercase chars from [0-9a-f]. Common contexts: file checksums, password hashes (broken — never use for security), Git tree IDs (SHA1, 40 chars). Easy to spot a hash by length: 32 = MD5, 40 = SHA1, 56 = SHA224, 64 = SHA256, 96 = SHA384, 128 = SHA512, 64 with $argon2 prefix = Argon2 with salt embedded.

name: SHA-256 hex digest length recognition
explanation: SHA-256 produces a 256-bit (32-byte) hash. As a hex string it's exactly 64 lowercase chars from [0-9a-f]. Modern standard for file integrity (most package managers verify SHA-256), VirusTotal sample IDs, container image digests (sha256:...). Argon2id password hashes start with `$argon2id$...$` followed by base64-encoded 32-byte hash. bcrypt is 60 chars starting with `$2y$` or `$2b$`.

name: Common bcrypt password hash format
explanation: bcrypt password hashes are 60 ASCII chars starting with the version (`$2y$`, `$2b$`, `$2a$`), then the cost factor (`$12$` for 2^12 iterations), then a 22-char base64-encoded salt, then a 31-char base64-encoded hash. Variants are interoperable; cost 12-14 is current best practice. Recognise from the leading `$2`: that signals bcrypt, distinct from `$argon2id$` for Argon2 and `$5$` / `$6$` for SHA-256/512 crypt.

name: x64 indirect call through register
longer_pattern: FF D0 (call rax) or FF D7 (call rdi)
explanation:
FF Dr is x86_64 indirect call through register r:
  FF D0 = call rax
  FF D3 = call rbx
  FF D7 = call rdi
  FF D6 = call rsi
Common in: virtual function dispatch (vtable lookup into rax then call rax), function pointer calls, JIT-emitted code, ROP/JOP gadget chains. Direct function calls use E8 + 4-byte relative offset, which the linker resolves at static link time. Indirect calls through fixed addresses are harder to track statically.

name: x64 syscall instruction (Linux ABI)
explanation:
0F 05 is the x86_64 SYSCALL instruction. The Linux syscall ABI uses rax = number, rdi/rsi/rdx/r10/r8/r9 as args 1-6. Common preludes:
  B8 01 00 00 00 0F 05    ; sys_write
  B8 02 00 00 00 0F 05    ; sys_open
  B8 3B 00 00 00 0F 05    ; sys_execve
  B8 E7 00 00 00 0F 05    ; sys_exit_group (231)
macOS x86_64 also uses SYSCALL but with BSD-style numbers + 0x2000000 offset. Windows uses int 0x2E or syscall via ntdll wrapper, not direct.
